1.question: For a short transmission line, the ABCD constants are:
options: A = 0, B = Z, C = Y, D = 0
A = D = 1 + ZY/2, B = Z, C = Y
1.explanation:
A short line neglects the shunt admittance, so the sending-end and receiving-end currents are equal and Vs = Vr + Z Ir. So A = 1, B = Z, C = 0, D = 1.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ A = D = 1, B = 0, C = Y: Shunt-only network (a capacitor), with no series impedance.
(b) ✘ A = 0, B = Z, C = Y, D = 0: A = D = 0 is not a transmission line; a short line has A = D = 1.
(c) ✘ A = D = 1 + ZY/2, B = Z, C = Y: Constants of a nominal-π medium line.
(d) ✔ A = D = 1, B = Z, C = 0: correct answer.

1.question: In the nominal-π representation of a medium-length transmission line:
options: The shunt admittance is neglected and the series impedance is halved
Half of the total shunt admittance is placed at each end of the line
The series impedance is split into two halves and the shunt admittance is placed between them
The whole shunt admittance is placed at the middle of the line
1.explanation:
The π model has the series impedance Z in the middle and Y/2 at each end. The T model splits Z into two halves with the whole Y in the middle (the last option describes the T model).

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The shunt admittance is neglected and the series impedance…: Describes the short-line model (Y neglected).
(b) ✔ Half of the total shunt admittance is placed at each end of…: correct answer.
(c) ✘ The series impedance is split into two halves and the shunt…: Describes the nominal-T model (Z split in halves around the shunt).
(d) ✘ The whole shunt admittance is placed at the middle of the l…: Not a standard model; the T model puts the whole Y in the middle with Z split.

1.question: The Ferranti effect (receiving-end voltage higher than the sending-end voltage) is most pronounced in:
options: A short, heavily loaded line with a lagging power factor
A short line fed through a transformer with taps
A long, lightly loaded or open-circuited line, because of the line charging current
A long, heavily loaded line with a lagging power factor
1.explanation:
The charging current flows through the line inductance and produces a voltage rise in phase with the receiving-end voltage. The effect increases with the square of the line length and is largest on no-load.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ A short, heavily loaded line with a lagging power factor: Short heavily loaded lagging line: the voltage drops.
(b) ✘ A short line fed through a transformer with taps: A tap-changing transformer regulates voltage; it is not the Ferranti condition.
(c) ✔ A long, lightly loaded or open-circuited line, because of t…: correct answer.
(d) ✘ A long, heavily loaded line with a lagging power factor: Heavily loaded lagging line: the voltage drops; there is no rise.

1.question: A line has an open-circuit receiving-end voltage of 33.6 kV and a full-load receiving-end voltage of 32 kV when the sending-end voltage is held constant. The voltage regulation is:
1.explanation:
Regulation = (|Vr,NL| − |Vr,FL|)/|Vr,FL| × 100 = (33.6 − 32)/32 × 100 = 5%. Dividing by the no-load voltage would give 4.76%, which is not the definition.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 5%: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 4.8%: Divides by the no-load voltage (1.6/33.6).
(c) ✘ 95%: Is the ratio of full-load to no-load voltage (32/33.6).
(d) ✘ 1.6%: Is the voltage difference in kV, not a percentage.

1.question: A lossless line has A = D = 0.95 and B = j50 Ω. Using AD − BC = 1 (reciprocal network), the constant C is:
1.explanation:
BC = AD − 1 = 0.9025 − 1 = −0.0975. C = −0.0975/(j50) = j0.00195 S (since 1/j = −j). C is positive imaginary (capacitive), as expected for the shunt charging of a line.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ −j0.00195 S: Wrong sign; 1/j = −j gives a positive imaginary C.
(b) ✘ j0.0195 S: Decimal slip, ten times too large.
(c) ✔ j0.00195 S: correct answer.
(d) ✘ j0.00098 S: Half the value; BC was mis-evaluated.

2.question: A 33 kV (line-to-line) short three-phase line supplies 10 MW at 0.8 power factor lagging at the receiving end. The line impedance is (5 + j10) Ω per phase. The voltage regulation of the line is approximately:
2.explanation:
I = 10 × 10⁶ / (√3 × 33 × 10³ × 0.8) = 218.7 A. Vr (phase) = 19.05 kV. Taking Vr as reference, Ir = 218.7(0.8 − j0.6) A. Drop = Ir(5 + j10) = 218.7 × (10 + j5) = 2187 + j1093 V. Vs = 19 053 + 2187 + j1093 = 21 240 + j1093 V, so |Vs| = 21.27 kV per phase. Regulation = (21.27 − 19.05)/19.05 = 11.6%. The approximate formula I(R cos φ + X sin φ)/Vr gives 11.5%.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 11.6%: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 13.9%: Right for a load of about 12 MW.
(c) ✘ 15.0%: Right for a load of about 12.9 MW.
(d) ✘ 9.1%: Right for a load of about 7.8 MW.

2.question: A lossless 3-phase line has a phase constant β = 0.001 rad/km and a length of 300 km. With the receiving end open (no-load) and the sending-end voltage held constant, the rise in the receiving-end voltage (Ferranti effect) is approximately:
2.explanation:
For a lossless line, Vr = Vs / cos βl. βl = 0.3 rad, cos 0.3 = 0.9553, so Vr/Vs = 1.0468, a rise of 4.7%. The rise is proportional to l² (for small βl, ≈ (βl)²/2 = 4.5%).

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 30%: Misreads βl = 0.3 rad as 30%.
(b) ✘ 0.3%: Misreads the formula; the rise is about (βl)²/2, not βl/100.
(c) ✔ 4.7%: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 9.4%: Double: right for a line of about 424 km (rise ∝ l²).

2.question: A nominal-π model of a medium line has Z = 60∠75° Ω and Y = j4 × 10⁻⁴ S. The ABCD parameter A = 1 + ZY/2 is approximately:
2.explanation:
ZY = 60 × 4 × 10⁻⁴ ∠(75° + 90°) = 0.024∠165°. ZY/2 = 0.012∠165° = −0.01159 + j0.00311. A = 1 + ZY/2 = 0.98841 + j0.00311 = 0.988∠0.18°. Using 1 − ZY/2 would give 1.012.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 1.012∠−0.18°: Right for A = 1 − ZY/2.
(b) ✔ 0.988∠0.18°: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 1.012∠0.18°: Magnitude above 1 with a positive angle is not possible: ZY/2 has a negative real part here, so A is below 1.
(d) ✘ 0.988∠75°: Right magnitude but the angle of Z, not of A.

2.question: Two identical lossless lines with A = D = 0.9 (real) and B = j100 Ω, with AD − BC = 1, are connected in cascade. The constant A of the combined network (A_eq = A² + BC) is:
2.explanation:
From AD − BC = 1: BC = A² − 1 = 0.81 − 1 = −0.19. Then A_eq = A² + BC = 0.81 − 0.19 = 0.62 (also = 2A² − 1). A_eq cannot be simply A² = 0.81 because the B C product also contributes.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 1.80: Is the sum 2A, not the cascade value.
(b) ✘ 0.45: Half of A (0.9/2).
(c) ✘ 0.81: Is A² only; the BC term is left out.
(d) ✔ 0.62: correct answer.

2.question: For a nominal-π model of a lossless line, B = Z = j100 Ω and the total shunt admittance is Y = j0.002 S. The constant C = Y(1 + ZY/4) is:
2.explanation:
ZY = j100 × j0.002 = −0.2. C = j0.002 (1 − 0.2/4) = j0.002 × 0.95 = j0.0019 S. The result is slightly smaller than Y because, in a lossless inductive line, ZY is negative.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ j0.0010 S: Is Y/2, the shunt at each end of the π.
(b) ✘ j0.0021 S: Uses 1 + ZY/4 = 1.05 with the wrong sign.
(c) ✘ j0.0020 S: Is Y itself (the short-line approximation).
(d) ✔ j0.0019 S: correct answer.

2.question: A medium line is represented by the nominal-T model with total series impedance Z = j80 Ω and total shunt admittance Y = j1 × 10⁻³ S. The constants A and B are:
2.explanation:
For the nominal-T model: A = D = 1 + YZ/2 and B = Z (1 + YZ/4). YZ = (j10⁻³)(j80) = −0.08. A = 1 − 0.04 = 0.96. B = j80 (1 − 0.02) = j78.4 Ω. (C = Y (1 + YZ/4) = j0.98 × 10⁻³ S.)

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ A = 0.92, B = j76.8 Ω: Uses A = 1 + YZ (not YZ/2).
(b) ✘ A = 1.04, B = j81.6 Ω: Sign error: A = 1 − YZ/2 would give 1.04.
(c) ✘ A = 0.96, B = j80 Ω: B left as Z; the factor (1 + YZ/4) is missing.
(d) ✔ A = 0.96, B = j78.4 Ω: correct answer.

2.question: A lossless three-phase line has A = D = 0.95 and B = j90 Ω. It delivers 100 MW at unity power factor at a receiving-end voltage of 220 kV (line to line). The sending-end line voltage is approximately:
2.explanation:
Vr = 220/√3 = 127.02 kV; Ir = 100 × 10⁶/(√3 × 220 × 10³) = 262.4 A at 0° (unity pf). Vs = A Vr + B Ir = 0.95 × 127 017 + j90 × 262.4 = 120 666 + j23 616 V. |Vs| = 122.96 kV per phase, so the line value is √3 × 122.96 = 213 kV.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 225 kV: Right for a load of about 200 MW.
(b) ✔ 213 kV: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 233 kV: Right for a load of about 250 MW.
(d) ✘ 209 kV: Is A × Vr only (209 kV); the B × Ir term is ignored.

2.question: A 132 kV three-phase line has B = 50∠75° Ω. With the sending end held at the rated voltage and the receiving end short-circuited, the sending-end current is approximately:
2.explanation:
With Vr = 0, Vs = B Ir, so the short-circuit current Isc = Vs/B = (132 000/√3)/50 = 76 210/50 = 1524 A (lagging the voltage by 75°). Using the line voltage instead of the phase voltage would give 2640 A.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 2640 A: Uses the line voltage 132 kV instead of the phase voltage.
(b) ✘ 1099 A: Right for B = 69 Ω.
(c) ✔ 1524 A: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 762 A: Right for B = 100 Ω.

2.question: A short three-phase line of resistance 1.5 Ω per phase delivers 5 MW at 0.9 power factor lagging at 11 kV (line to line). Neglecting the reactance, the transmission efficiency is approximately:
2.explanation:
I = 5 × 10⁶/(√3 × 11 × 10³ × 0.9) = 291.6 A. Loss = 3 I² R = 3 × (291.6)² × 1.5 = 382.6 kW. Efficiency = 5/(5 + 0.3826) × 100 = 92.9%.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 92.9%: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 96.3%: Right for a resistance of about 0.75 Ω.
(c) ✘ 98.2%: Right for a resistance of about 0.36 Ω.
(d) ✘ 89.7%: Right for a resistance of about 2.25 Ω.

2.question: A short line has Z = 4 + j12 Ω per phase and supplies a load current of 100 A at 0.8 power factor leading at a receiving-end phase voltage of 6350 V. The voltage regulation is approximately:
2.explanation:
For a leading load I = 100(0.8 + j0.6) = 80 + j60 A. Vs = Vr + I Z = 6350 + (80 + j60)(4 + j12) = 6350 + (320 − 720) + j(960 + 240) = 5950 + j1200. |Vs| = 6070 V. Regulation = (|Vs| − |Vr|)/|Vr| = (6070 − 6350)/6350 = −4.4%. A negative regulation means the voltage rises at the load end.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ +4.4% (voltage drops at the load): Right magnitude but wrong sign: a leading load gives a voltage rise.
(b) ✘ +9.2%: Not from the vector sum Vs = Vr + IZ.
(c) ✔ −4.4% (voltage rises at the load): correct answer.
(d) ✘ −9.2%: Not from the vector sum Vs = Vr + IZ; the sign and size are both wrong.

1.question: A lossless line of reactance X = 0.5 pu joins two buses with |Vs| = |Vr| = 1.0 pu and a power angle δ = 30°. The real power transmitted is:
1.explanation:
P = |Vs||Vr| sin δ / X = 1 × 1 × sin 30° / 0.5 = 0.5/0.5 = 1.0 pu.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.5 pu: Forgets to divide by X.
(b) ✔ 1.0 pu: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 0.866 pu: Uses cos δ instead of sin δ.
(d) ✘ 2.0 pu: Is the maximum (1/X, δ = 90°).

1.question: A 400 kV (line-to-line) lossless line has a total series reactance of 80 Ω. With |Vs| = |Vr| = 400 kV, the theoretical maximum real power that can be transmitted (δ = 90°) is:
1.explanation:
Pmax = |Vs||Vr| / X = (400 × 10³)² / 80 = 2 × 10⁹ W = 2000 MW (using line-to-line voltages in the three-phase formula).

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 4000 MW: Right if X were 40 Ω.
(b) ✘ 500 MW: Right if X were 320 Ω.
(c) ✘ 1000 MW: Right if X were 160 Ω.
(d) ✔ 2000 MW: correct answer.

1.question: In a high-voltage transmission line whose resistance is negligible compared with its reactance, the main factor controlling the real power flow and the main factor controlling the reactive power flow are respectively:
options: The angle δ between the end voltages; the voltage magnitude difference
The line resistance; the line shunt capacitance of the line
The line shunt capacitance; the line resistance of the line
The voltage magnitude difference; the angle δ between the end voltages
1.explanation:
P ≈ (|Vs||Vr|/X) sin δ depends mainly on δ, and Q ≈ (|Vr|/X)(|Vs| cos δ − |Vr|) depends mainly on the voltage difference. This P–δ, Q–V coupling is the basis of the decoupled load flow.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ The angle δ between the end voltages; the voltage magnitude…: correct answer.
(b) ✘ The line resistance; the line shunt capacitance of the line: Resistance is negligible, so it does not control P; capacitance is not the main Q control.
(c) ✘ The line shunt capacitance; the line resistance of the line: Reversed and wrong: neither is the main control.
(d) ✘ The voltage magnitude difference; the angle δ between the e…: Reversed: P follows δ and Q follows the voltage difference.

1.question: A lossless line of X = 0.5 pu has |Vs| = 1.0 pu, |Vr| = 0.95 pu and δ = 10°. The reactive power Qr received at the receiving end is approximately:
1.explanation:
Qr = (|Vr|/X)(|Vs| cos δ − |Vr|) = (0.95/0.5)(0.9848 − 0.95) = 1.9 × 0.0348 = 0.066 pu, positive, so reactive power is delivered to the receiving end.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ −0.066 pu: Right if |Vr| were larger than |Vs| cos δ (reactive flow reversed).
(b) ✘ 0.0 pu: Right if |Vs| cos δ equalled |Vr|.
(c) ✔ 0.066 pu: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 0.348 pu: Not from the correct formula (cos δ misused).

1.question: Series capacitors are inserted to compensate 30% of the line reactance. For the same end voltages and the same power angle, the real power transmitted increases by about:
1.explanation:
The new reactance is 0.7 X, so P ∝ 1/X increases by a factor 1/0.7 = 1.4286, i.e. 42.9%. (30% would be a mistake of treating the reduction as the increase.)

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 30%: Treats the reduction in reactance as the increase in power.
(b) ✔ 42.9%: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 23.1%: Is the fall in P if the reactance had increased by 30%.
(d) ✘ 70%: Is the reactance that remains, not the change in power.

2.question: A gen of 0.1 pu reactace conneted to a Infinite bus through T/F and T/L with 0.2 and 0.1 pu of reactance calculate Pmax if (1) Vg = 1.6 pu and (2) Vt = 1.6 pu assume 𝑽∞ = 1 pu ?

A lossless line has a reactance of 0.4 pu on a 100 MVA base. The sending-end voltage is 1.1 pu and the receiving-end voltage is 1.0 pu. The maximum power that can be transferred (steady-state limit) is:
2.explanation:
Pmax = |Vs||Vr|/X = 1.1 × 1.0/0.4 = 2.75 pu = 275 MW (at δ = 90°).

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 275 MW: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 250 MW: Right if both voltages were 1.0 pu.
(c) ✘ 300 MW: Right for X = 0.367 pu.
(d) ✘ 110 MW: Is 1.1 × 100 only; X is ignored.

2.question: Two lossless lines of reactances 0.4 pu and 0.6 pu are connected in parallel between two buses with |Vs| = |Vr| = 1.0 pu. The power transferred at a power angle of 30° (100 MVA base) is:
2.explanation:
Xeq = (0.4 × 0.6)/(0.4 + 0.6) = 0.24 pu. P = (1 × 1/0.24) sin 30° = 4.167 × 0.5 = 2.083 pu = 208.3 MW.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 416.7 MW: Is the maximum (δ = 90°), with sin 30° ignored.
(b) ✘ 125 MW: Uses only the 0.4 pu line.
(c) ✔ 208.3 MW: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 83.3 MW: Uses only the 0.6 pu line.

2.question: A 220 kV lossless line can transmit at most 150 MW. The same line (same reactance) is operated at 400 kV with the same power-angle limit. The new steady-state limit is approximately:
2.explanation:
Pmax = V²/X, so it varies with the square of the voltage. Pmax(400 kV) = 150 × (400/220)² = 150 × 3.306 = 496 MW. (Scaling directly with the voltage would give 273 MW, which is wrong.)

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 150 MW: Right if the voltage were unchanged.
(b) ✔ 496 MW: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 273 MW: Scales with V instead of V².
(d) ✘ 825 MW: Not a valid scaling.

2.question: A three-phase line of impedance (3 + j24) Ω per phase operates at |Vs| = |Vr| = 33 kV (line to line) and supplies a load at 0.9 power factor leading. The active power delivered is approximately:
2.explanation:
Equal end voltages are possible only for a leading load. With Vph = 19 053 V, I = 2 Vph (X sinφ − R cosφ)/(R² + X²) = 2 × 19 053 × (24 × 0.4359 − 3 × 0.9)/585 = 505.6 A. P = √3 × 33 kV × 505.6 × 0.9 = 26.0 MW.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 21.3 MW: Right for a current of about 414 A.
(b) ✘ 15.5 MW: Right for a current of about 300 A.
(c) ✘ 31.9 MW: Right for a current of about 620 A.
(d) ✔ 26.0 MW: correct answer.

2.question: A lossless line carries power P = Pmax sin δ and operates at δ = 30°. The steady-state stability margin, (Pmax − P)/Pmax, is:
2.explanation:
P/Pmax = sin 30° = 0.5. Margin = (Pmax − P)/Pmax = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5 = 50%. The margin is the part of the maximum power that is still available before reaching δ = 90°.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 60%: Right at δ = 24.1° (sin δ = 0.4).
(b) ✘ 30%: Right at δ = 44.4° (sin δ = 0.7).
(c) ✘ 70%: Right at δ = 17.5° (sin δ = 0.3).
(d) ✔ 50%: correct answer.

1.question: Shunt reactors are sometimes used in high voltage transmission systems to
options: limit the short circuit current through the line.
compensate for the series reactance of the line under heavily loaded condition.
limit over voltages at the load side under lightly loaded condition.
compensate for the voltage drop in the line
1.explanation:
Due to ferranti effect Vr > Vs occurs in light load / no load  conditions in medium and long lines

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ limit the short circuit current through the line: That is the role of series reactors.
(b) ✘ compensate for the series reactance of the line under heavi…: That is the role of series capacitors.
(c) ✔ limit over voltages at the load side under lightly loaded c…: correct answer.
(d) ✘ compensate for the voltage drop in the line: That is the role of shunt capacitors.

1.question: Reactive power flows in an inductive transmission line mainly from the bus with:
options: The lower voltage magnitude to the higher voltage magnitude
The leading phase angle to the lagging phase angle
The higher voltage magnitude to the bus with the lower voltage magnitude
The lagging phase angle to the leading phase angle
1.explanation:
For a line with small δ, Q ≈ (V1/X)(V1 − V2): reactive power goes from the higher to the lower voltage magnitude, while the real power goes from the leading to the lagging angle.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The lower voltage magnitude to the higher voltage magnitude: Reversed.
(b) ✘ The leading phase angle to the lagging phase angle: This describes the direction of real power.
(c) ✔ The higher voltage magnitude to the bus with the lower volt…: correct answer.
(d) ✘ The lagging phase angle to the leading phase angle: Reverse of the real power direction.

1.question: A shunt capacitor bank delivers 6 MVAr (3-phase) at a bus of a 33 kV system. The Thevenin reactance of the system at the bus is 10 Ω. The approximate rise in bus voltage (line-to-line) is:
1.explanation:
ΔV ≈ Q X/V = (6 × 10⁶ × 10)/(33 × 10³) = 1818 V = 1.82 kV (line-to-line). This is about 5.5% of the system voltage.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 1.82 kV: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 6.0 kV: Reads the MVAr value as kV.
(c) ✘ 18.2 kV: Decimal slip, ten times too large.
(d) ✘ 0.18 kV: Decimal slip, ten times too small.

1.question: An on-load tap changer has a range of ±10% in 16 equal steps. The voltage change per tap step is:
1.explanation:
Total range = 20% (from −10% to +10%) divided into 16 steps: 20/16 = 1.25% per step.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 2.5%: Is 20/8 (8 steps).
(b) ✘ 0.625%: Is 20/32 (32 steps).
(c) ✘ 1.0%: Right for 20 steps.
(d) ✔ 1.25%: correct answer.

1.question: An over-excited synchronous condenser connected to a bus:
options: Neither supplies nor absorbs reactive power
Supplies lagging reactive power to the system and raises the bus voltage
Supplies real power to the system and raises the frequency
Absorbs lagging reactive power and lowers the bus voltage
1.explanation:
An over-excited synchronous machine (running without a load) behaves as a capacitor and delivers lagging vars to the system, raising the voltage at heavy load. At light load it is run under-excited to absorb vars and limit the voltage rise. It also contributes to the short-circuit level and the inertia.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Neither supplies nor absorbs reactive power: Right for a machine at neutral excitation (floating).
(b) ✔ Supplies lagging reactive power to the system and raises th…: correct answer.
(c) ✘ Supplies real power to the system and raises the frequency: A synchronous condenser has no prime mover and supplies no real power.
(d) ✘ Absorbs lagging reactive power and lowers the bus voltage: Right for an under-excited condenser.

1.question: A 3-phase capacitor bank is rated 3 MVAr at 11 kV. When the bus voltage is only 10 kV, the reactive power it supplies is approximately:
1.explanation:
Q ∝ V² for a constant capacitance. Q = 3 × (10/11)² = 2.48 MVAr. The support of the capacitor decreases when the voltage is low, as the lower voltage reduces its output more than proportionally.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 2.48 MVAr: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 2.73 MVAr: Wrong: Q varies as V², not V.
(c) ✘ 3.00 MVAr: Right at the rated 11 kV.
(d) ✘ 3.30 MVAr: Right at about 11.5 kV (above rated).

2.question: find 𝑷(𝟑∅)  𝒊𝒇 Vs =Vr = 11 KV , Z = 3 + j4 , pf = 0.8 lag at load end
A transmission line has an impedance of (3 + j 4) ohms/phase. The PF. of the load required for maximum and zero voltage regulation are respectively?
2.explanation:
Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.6 lead, 0.6 lag: Maximum regulation occurs at a lagging pf, not a leading one.
(b) ✘ 0.6 lag, 0.6 lead: Zero regulation needs 0.8 leading (tanφ = R/X = 0.75).
(c) ✔ 0.6 lag, 0.8 lead: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 0.8 lag, 0.6 lead: Swaps the two: 0.8 leading is for zero regulation.

2.question: A feeder with reactance of 0.2 p.u. has a sens o end voltage of 1.2 p.u. If the reactive power Supplied at receiving-end of the feeder is 0.3 p.u. the approximate voltage drop in feeder in pu will be     (IAS1999)

1.question: surge impedance of a transmission line of length 200 km is 400 ohms. If the length of the line is doubled then the Surge impedance of the line in ohms is
1.explanation:
Surge impedance is independent of length of line and hence answer is 400 ohms

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 800: Would hold if Zc grew with length; it does not (L and C both scale with length).
(b) ✘ 200: Would hold if Zc fell with length; it does not.
(c) ✔ 400: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 1000: Not a combination of the data; Zc is independent of length.

1.question: For a loss less line
1.explanation:
R=G=0

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ R=G= 0,: correct answer.
(b) ✘ R= 0, G is non zero: Describes leakage (dielectric) loss only.
(c) ✘ R is non Zero, G = 0: Describes conductor loss only.
(d) ✘ Both are Non Zero: Describes a lossy line.

2.question: A 400 kV (line-to-line) lossless line has L = 1.3 mH/km and C = 9 nF/km. Its surge impedance loading (SIL) is approximately:
2.explanation:
Zc = √(L/C) = √(1.3 × 10⁻³/9 × 10⁻⁹) = 380 Ω. SIL = V²/Zc = (400 × 10³)²/380 = 421 MW (V is line-to-line).

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 526 MW: Is the SIL after 36% series compensation.
(b) ✘ 380 MW: Is Zc in ohms, not SIL.
(c) ✔ 421 MW: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 400 MW: Is the voltage in kV.

2.question: The line of the previous data (Zc = 380 Ω, SIL = 421 MW at 400 kV) is compensated with series capacitors of 36%. Since Zc′ = Zc √(1 − k), the new SIL is approximately:
2.explanation:
Zc′ = 380 × √(1 − 0.36) = 380 × 0.8 = 304 Ω. SIL′ = 400²/304 = 526 MW = 421/0.8. Series compensation lowers the surge impedance and so raises the SIL.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 526 MW: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 421 MW: Is the uncompensated SIL.
(c) ✘ 658 MW: Divides by (1 − k) instead of √(1 − k).
(d) ✘ 337 MW: Multiplies by 0.8: the SIL rises with series compensation, it does not fall.

2.question: A 400 kV lossless line (Zc = 380 Ω, SIL = 421 MW) has 19% shunt reactor compensation, which reduces the effective shunt capacitance to C(1 − 0.19). The new SIL is approximately:
2.explanation:
Zc′ = Zc/√(1 − k_sh) = 380/0.9 = 422 Ω. SIL′ = 400²/422 = 379 MW = 0.9 × 421. Shunt (inductive) compensation raises the surge impedance and lowers the SIL; series (capacitive) compensation does the opposite.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 421 MW: Right if there were no compensation.
(b) ✘ 341 MW: Multiplies by 0.81 (= 1 − k) instead of 0.9.
(c) ✘ 468 MW: Right for series capacitor compensation (421/0.9).
(d) ✔ 379 MW: correct answer.

2.question: For a lossless line loaded to less than its SIL, which of the following is correct?
options: The line absorbs net reactive power and the receiving-end voltage falls
The line generates net reactive power and the receiving-end voltage tends to rise
The line generates reactive power and the voltage at the receiving end falls
The line neither generates nor absorbs reactive power
2.explanation:
At the SIL the reactive power generated by the line capacitance equals the I²X absorbed by the series reactance, giving a flat voltage profile. Below SIL, the capacitive generation exceeds the inductive absorption, so the line is a net source of vars and the voltage rises (Ferranti effect); above SIL it is a net absorber and the voltage falls.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The line absorbs net reactive power and the receiving-end v…: Right above the SIL: the line absorbs net vars and the voltage falls.
(b) ✔ The line generates net reactive power and the receiving-end…: correct answer.
(c) ✘ The line generates reactive power and the voltage at the re…: Not consistent: net reactive generation makes the voltage rise.
(d) ✘ The line neither generates nor absorbs reactive power: Right exactly at the SIL.

2.question: A lossless line has L = 1.3 mH/km and C = 9 nF/km. The velocity of propagation of the waves on the line is approximately:
2.explanation:
v = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(1.3 × 10⁻³ × 9 × 10⁻⁹) = 1/√(1.17 × 10⁻¹¹) = 2.92 × 10⁸ m/s = 2.92 × 10⁵ km/s, close to (and slightly below) the speed of light, which is typical of overhead lines.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 2.9 × 10⁵ km/s: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 2.9 × 10³ km/s: Decimal slip, a thousand times too small.
(c) ✘ 1.5 × 10⁵ km/s: Right if LC were four times larger (half the speed).
(d) ✘ 3.0 × 10⁵ km/s: Is the speed of light; lines are slightly below.

2.question: A 220 kV line with a surge impedance of 400 Ω has SIL = 121 MW. If the line is operated at 0.9 pu voltage (198 kV), its SIL becomes approximately:
2.explanation:
SIL = V²/Zc, so it varies with the square of the voltage. SIL = 121 × 0.9² = 98.0 MW. Check: 198²/400 = 98.0 MW.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 121 MW: Is the SIL at rated voltage (no change).
(b) ✔ 98 MW: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 134 MW: Right at 1.05 pu voltage (V²).
(d) ✘ 109 MW: Scales linearly with V (0.9 × 121).

2.question: A 400 kV line has Zc = 380 Ω and SIL = 421 MW. It is compensated with 30% series capacitance and 20% shunt inductance. The new surge impedance and SIL are approximately:
2.explanation:
Zc,new = Zc √[(1 − k_series)/(1 − k_shunt)] = 380 √(0.7/0.8) = 355.5 Ω. SIL,new = 400²/355.5 = 450 MW. Series compensation lowers Zc, shunt compensation raises it; here the net effect is a lower Zc.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 380 Ω and 421 MW: Uncompensated values.
(b) ✘ 342 Ω and 468 MW: Right for 19% series compensation alone.
(c) ✘ 406 Ω and 394 MW: Right for shunt compensation alone of about 12%.
(d) ✔ 355.5 Ω and 450 MW: correct answer.

2.question: An underground cable has L = 0.35 mH/km and C = 0.25 μF/km. Its surge impedance and its SIL at 66 kV (line to line) are approximately:
2.explanation:
Zc = √(L/C) = √(0.35 × 10⁻³/0.25 × 10⁻⁶) = √1400 = 37.4 Ω. SIL = V²/Zc = 66²/37.4 = 116 MW. Cables have a much lower Zc than overhead lines, so their SIL is high but they are normally loaded far below it because of their large charging current.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 37.4 Ω and 116 MW: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 37.4 Ω and 1.16 MW: Decimal slip in the SIL.
(c) ✘ 1.18 Ω and 3700 MW: Decimal slip (√1.4 instead of √1400).
(d) ✘ 374 Ω and 11.6 MW: Decimal slip: Zc ten times too large.

2.question: A lossless line has a velocity of propagation of 3 × 10⁵ km/s at 50 Hz. The electrical length of a 750 km line, in degrees, is:
2.explanation:
Wavelength λ = v/f = 3 × 10⁵/50 = 6000 km. Electrical angle = 360° × 750/6000 = 45°. (This is β l with β = 2π/λ.)

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 60°: Right for a 1000 km line.
(b) ✘ 90°: Right for a 1500 km line.
(c) ✔ 45°: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 22.5°: Right for a 375 km line.

2.question: A lossless line has β = 0.0012 rad/km and is 250 km long. When it is open-circuited at the receiving end with a sending-end voltage of 400 kV, the receiving-end voltage is approximately:
2.explanation:
β l = 0.0012 × 250 = 0.3 rad. For an open-circuited lossless line Vr = Vs/cos βl = 400/cos(0.3) = 400/0.9553 = 418.7 kV. This voltage rise at the open end is the Ferranti effect.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 436 kV: Right for a line of about 340 km.
(b) ✔ 419 kV: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 400 kV: Right if βl were zero (no rise) or for a loaded line.
(d) ✘ 382 kV: Is a voltage fall (400 cos 0.3); an open end rises.

conventional.question: What is SIL ? Derive the expression on Surge Impedance Loading  ?
conventional.explanation:
SIL = Surge Impedance Loading. It is the three-phase active power loading of a transmission line at which the
reactive power generated by the line's shunt capacitance is equal to the reactive power absorbed by the line's series
inductance.
At SIL, the line is approximately reactively balanced: the net reactive power exchange of the line is approximately
zero under the idealized long-line condition. SIL is therefore a useful reference level for discussing voltage behaviour
and natural loading of transmission lines.

1.question: A load of 500 kW operates at 0.7 power factor lagging. If the power factor is improved to 0.95 lagging, the reduction in the kVA demand is approximately:
1.explanation:
Initial kVA = 500/0.7 = 714.3 kVA. Final kVA = 500/0.95 = 526.3 kVA. Reduction = 714.3 − 526.3 = 188 kVA.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 214 kVA: Right for improving to unity pf (714.3 − 500).
(b) ✘ 412 kVA: Not a difference of the two kVA values.
(c) ✔ 188 kVA: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 98 kVA: Right for improving 0.70 to about 0.81.

1.question: A 200 kVA load at 0.7 power factor lagging is supplied together with a synchronous motor that takes 60 kW at 0.8 power factor leading. The overall power factor is approximately:
1.explanation:
Load 1: P = 140 kW, Q = 200 × 0.714 = 142.8 kVAr (lag). Motor: P = 60 kW, Q = 60 × 0.75 = 45 kVAr (lead). Total P = 200 kW, Q = 142.8 − 45 = 97.8 kVAr, S = 222.6 kVA. pf = 200/222.6 = 0.90 lagging.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 0.90 lagging: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 0.70 lagging: Is the pf of the load alone.
(c) ✘ 0.80 leading: Is the motor's own pf, not the combined one.
(d) ✘ 0.95 lagging: Needs more leading kVAr than the motor supplies.

1.question: A 415 V, 3-phase, 150 kW load works at 0.75 power factor lagging. It is to be improved to 0.95 lagging with a star-connected capacitor bank. The capacitance required per phase is approximately:
1.explanation:
Q = 150 (tan φ1 − tan φ2) = 150 (0.8819 − 0.3287) = 83.0 kVAr. Per phase 27.66 kVAr. Vph = 415/√3 = 239.6 V. C = Q_ph/(ω Vph²) = 27 660/(314.16 × 57 408) = 1.534 × 10⁻³ F = 1534 μF.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 4600 μF: Is three times the star value.
(b) ✘ 511 μF: Is the value for a delta-connected bank (a third).
(c) ✘ 153 μF: Decimal slip, ten times too small.
(d) ✔ 1534 μF: correct answer.

1.question: A 400 kW load at 0.8 power factor lagging has a 150 kVAr capacitor bank connected in parallel. The new power factor is approximately:
1.explanation:
Q before = 400 × tan(36.87°) = 300 kVAr. Q after = 300 − 150 = 150 kVAr. tan φ = 150/400 = 0.375, so cos φ = 0.936 lagging.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.80 lagging: Is the pf without the capacitor.
(b) ✔ 0.936 lagging: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 0.60 lagging: Right only if the lagging kVAr had increased.
(d) ✘ 0.97 leading: Needs over-compensation (a bank above 300 kVAr).

1.question: When a shunt capacitor is connected at a load to improve the power factor (the load itself unchanged), which of the following remains unchanged?
options: The active power (kW) drawn by the load
The kVA supplied by the source
The voltage drop in the feeder
1.explanation:
The capacitor supplies reactive power only. The line current, the kVA and the feeder voltage drop and loss decrease, but the real power consumed by the load does not change.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ The active power (kW) drawn by the load: correct answer.
(b) ✘ The kVA supplied by the source: Decreases: the source supplies less reactive power.
(c) ✘ The line current: Decreases.
(d) ✘ The voltage drop in the feeder: Decreases.

2.question:
Shunt reactors are sometimes used in high
voltage transmission systems to
options: Limit the short circuit current through the line
compensate for the series resistance of the line under heavily loaded condition
limit over voltages at the load side under lightly loaded condition
compensate for the voltage drop in the line under heavily loaded condition
2.explanation:
A long, lightly loaded (or open-circuited) transmission line behaves like a capacitor and its receiving-end voltage rises above the sending-end voltage (Ferranti effect), because the line charging current flows through the line inductance. A shunt reactor absorbs lagging reactive power (and the line charging current), so it limits this over-voltage at the load end under light-load conditions. It is switched out under heavy load, when the voltage drop is the problem and shunt capacitors or series compensation are used instead. A shunt reactor does not limit short-circuit current (a series reactor does) and does not compensate series resistance.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Limit the short circuit current through the line: That is the role of series reactors.
(b) ✘ compensate for the series resistance of the line under heav…: Series capacitors compensate series reactance, not resistance.
(c) ✔ limit over voltages at the load side under lightly loaded c…: correct answer.
(d) ✘ compensate for the voltage drop in the line under heavily l…: Shunt capacitors compensate voltage drop under heavy load.

1.question: Corona on an overhead line begins when:
options: The line current exceeds the thermal limit of the conductor
The surface voltage gradient falls below 21 kV/cm (rms) in air
The line voltage exceeds the lightning impulse level of the line
The surface voltage gradient exceeds about 30 kV/cm (peak), the breakdown strength of air
1.explanation:
When the electric stress at the conductor surface exceeds about 30 kV/cm (peak) in air at normal conditions, the air ionises and glows (corona), producing power loss, radio interference and ozone.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The line current exceeds the thermal limit of the conductor: Thermal limit relates to heating, not corona.
(b) ✘ The surface voltage gradient falls below 21 kV/cm (rms) in…: Right if 'falls below' were 'exceeds' (21.1 kV/cm rms is the same as 30 kV/cm peak).
(c) ✘ The line voltage exceeds the lightning impulse level of the…: Impulse level relates to flashover insulation, not steady-voltage corona.
(d) ✔ The surface voltage gradient exceeds about 30 kV/cm (peak),…: correct answer.

1.question: Which one of the following changes will NOT help to reduce corona loss in a transmission line?
options: Reducing the spacing between the conductors
1.explanation:
The disruptive critical voltage Vc ∝ r ln(D/r) so a larger radius or a larger spacing D raises Vc. Bundling, or a hollow conductor, increases the effective radius and lowers the surface gradient. Reducing the spacing lowers Vc and so increases the corona.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Increasing the conductor diameter: Helps: a larger diameter lowers the surface gradient.
(b) ✔ Reducing the spacing between the conductors: correct answer.
(c) ✘ Using hollow conductors: Helps: hollow conductors give a larger radius for the same metal.
(d) ✘ Using bundled conductors: Helps: bundling raises the effective radius.

1.question: Using Peek's formula V_c = 21.1 m δ r ln(D/r) kV (rms, phase), the critical disruptive voltage for a conductor of radius 1 cm, spacing D = 3 m, m = 0.85 and δ = 1 is approximately:
1.explanation:
V_c = 21.1 × 0.85 × 1 × 1 × ln(300) = 17.94 × 5.704 = 102.3 kV (phase to neutral, rms). The value is multiplied by √3 to get the line value (≈177 kV), so 177 kV is the line-to-line critical voltage and not the phase value.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 177 kV: Is the line-to-line value (102 × √3).
(b) ✘ 21.1 kV: Is the constant in Peek's formula, not the result.
(c) ✔ 102 kV: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 61 kV: Right for m = 0.5 (a very rough, weathered conductor).

1.question: Corona loss on a transmission line is generally:
options: Much larger in foul (stormy or rainy) weather than in fair weather
The same in fair and foul weather
Lower in foul weather, because the air is wetter
1.explanation:
Water droplets on the conductor surface create points of high local stress and reduce the critical voltage by up to about 20–30%, so the loss in foul weather can be many times that in fair weather. Peek's formula gives the fair-weather loss; the loss in foul weather is estimated by using a lower m value.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ Much larger in foul (stormy or rainy) weather than in fair…: correct answer.
(b) ✘ The same in fair and foul weather: Right only for a short, low-voltage line below the corona onset.
(c) ✘ Lower in foul weather, because the air is wetter: Wet air does not help: droplets distort the field and lower the critical voltage.
(d) ✘ Highest in dry, calm weather: Dry, calm weather gives the lowest (fair-weather) loss.

1.question: Compared with a single conductor of the same total cross-section, the use of a two-conductor bundle per phase on an EHV line:
options: Raises the surface gradient but lowers the line capacitance
Raises the line reactance and the corona loss
Lowers the surface voltage gradient and the corona loss, and lowers the line reactance
Has no effect on either the corona or the reactance
1.explanation:
A bundle increases the effective radius (GMR and the equivalent radius for the capacitance), so the surface gradient decreases, corona loss and radio noise decrease, the inductive reactance per phase decreases and the SIL increases.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Raises the surface gradient but lowers the line capacitance: A bundle lowers the surface gradient; this is right for a thinner single conductor.
(b) ✘ Raises the line reactance and the corona loss: Right for a single smaller conductor, not a bundle.
(c) ✔ Lowers the surface voltage gradient and the corona loss, an…: correct answer.
(d) ✘ Has no effect on either the corona or the reactance: Right only if the bundle spacing were so small that it acts as a single conductor.

2.question: A 3-phase 220 kV. 50 Hz transmission line consists of 2 cm radius conductor spaced 2.5m apart in equilateral triangular formulation. If the temperature is 20°C, atmospheric pressure 75 cm and irregularity factor (mo) = 0.80, then the corona loss per km of line is _____ kW. (Assume dielectric strength of air = 21.1 kV/cm(rms))

2.question: A 3-disc suspension insulator string has a ratio of pin-to-earth (shunt) capacitance to the self capacitance of a disc of k = 0.2. The string efficiency is approximately:
2.explanation:
Taking V1 across the top disc, V2 = V1(1 + k), V3 = V1(1 + 3k + k²). V = V1(3 + 4k + k²) = 3.84 V1 and V3 = 1.64 V1. String efficiency = V/(3 V3) = 3.84/(3 × 1.64) = 0.78.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 78%: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 66%: Right for k ≈ 0.4.
(c) ✘ 85%: Right for k ≈ 0.12.
(d) ✘ 92%: Right for k ≈ 0.05.

2.question: For the 3-disc string with k = 0.2 and a total voltage of 33 kV across the string, the voltage across the disc nearest to the line conductor is approximately:
2.explanation:
V1 = 33/3.84 = 8.59 kV. The line-end disc: V3 = 1.64 V1 = 14.09 kV. The ideal (equal) distribution would be 11 kV per disc; the line-end disc is the most heavily stressed.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 16.5 kV: Is half the total string voltage.
(b) ✘ 11.0 kV: Is the ideal equal share (33/3).
(c) ✔ 14.1 kV: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 8.6 kV: Is V1, the voltage across the top (cross-arm) disc.

2.question: A 132 kV transmission line uses suspension insulators in which each disc can withstand 11 kV. The string efficiency is 80%. The number of discs required per string (based on the phase voltage) is:
2.explanation:
Phase voltage = 132/√3 = 76.2 kV. Voltage per string that can be withstood = n × 11 × 0.80 (string efficiency). n = 76.2/(11 × 0.8) = 8.66, so 9 discs.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 7: Ignores the string efficiency (76.2/11 ≈ 7).
(b) ✔ 9: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 12: Uses the line voltage 132 kV with no efficiency (132/11 = 12).
(d) ✘ 8: Rounds 8.66 down; the number of discs must be rounded up.

2.question: Which of the following would increase the string efficiency of a suspension insulator string?
options: Using a shorter cross-arm on the tower
Increasing the pin-to-earth capacitance of the discs
Removing the grading ring at the line end
A longer cross-arm, giving less pin-to-earth capacitance
2.explanation:
String efficiency improves as the ratio k = (shunt capacitance)/(self capacitance) falls, so a longer cross-arm helps. Grading rings, capacitance grading (larger self-capacitance near the line end) and static shielding also help. Larger shunt capacitances worsen the distribution.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Using a shorter cross-arm on the tower: A shorter cross-arm raises the shunt capacitance and lowers the efficiency.
(b) ✘ Increasing the pin-to-earth capacitance of the discs: A larger shunt capacitance lowers the efficiency.
(c) ✘ Removing the grading ring at the line end: Removing the grading ring worsens the voltage distribution.
(d) ✔ A longer cross-arm, giving less pin-to-earth capacitance: correct answer.

2.question: A string of four discs has voltages of 6 kV, 8 kV, 11 kV and 15 kV across the individual discs. The string efficiency is approximately:
2.explanation:
String efficiency = (total voltage)/(n × voltage across the unit nearest the conductor) = 40/(4 × 15) = 0.667 = 66.7%.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 80%: Uses 12.5 kV instead of the highest disc voltage 15 kV.
(b) ✘ 40%: Is the total voltage in kV, not a percentage.
(c) ✘ 73.3%: Is 11/15: compares one disc with the maximum disc.
(d) ✔ 66.7%: correct answer.

1.question: A two-wire DC distributor is fed at one end at 250 V. It supplies loads of 30 A at 100 m and 20 A at 250 m from the feeding point. The resistance per conductor is 0.1 Ω/km. The voltage at the far load (250 m) is:
1.explanation:
Loop resistance = 0.2 Ω/km. Section 0–100 m carries 50 A: drop = 50 × 0.2 × 0.1 = 1.0 V. Section 100–250 m carries 20 A: drop = 20 × 0.2 × 0.15 = 0.6 V. V = 250 − 1.0 − 0.6 = 248.4 V.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 248.4 V: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 249.0 V: Counts only the first-section drop (1.0 V).
(c) ✘ 248.0 V: Right for a loop resistance of 0.25 Ω/km.
(d) ✘ 247.0 V: Right for a loop resistance of 0.375 Ω/km.

1.question: A 25 kVA single-phase transformer supplies a 230 V low-voltage distribution. The full-load secondary current is approximately:
1.explanation:
I = S/V = 25 000/230 = 108.7 A. (54.3 A would be the current at 460 V.)

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 54.3 A: Right at 460 V.
(b) ✘ 25 A: Reads the kVA value as amps.
(c) ✔ 108.7 A: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 217 A: Right at 115 V.

1.question: In a three-phase four-wire LV distribution system with a line voltage of 400 V, the voltage between a line and the neutral is approximately:
1.explanation:
V_phase = 400/√3 = 231 V ≈ 230 V. This allows both 400 V three-phase loads and 230 V single-phase loads to be supplied.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 693 V: Is 400 × √3, the wrong direction.
(b) ✔ 230 V: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 400 V: Is the line-to-line voltage.
(d) ✘ 115 V: Is half the phase voltage (115 V is a US single-phase supply).

1.question: A radial feeder differs from a ring main in that, in a radial feeder:
options: The fault level is always higher than in a ring main system
Each consumer has two supply paths, so no interruption occurs
The conductor must be heavier at the beginning than at the end
A fault interrupts supply to all consumers beyond the fault point
1.explanation:
A radial feeder has one supply path, so all loads beyond a faulty section lose supply until it is repaired. It is simple and cheap, but less reliable than a ring main or a network with alternative feeds.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The fault level is always higher than in a ring main system: Fault level is generally lower in a radial feeder, higher in a ring.
(b) ✘ Each consumer has two supply paths, so no interruption occu…: Describes a ring main (two supply paths).
(c) ✘ The conductor must be heavier at the beginning than at the…: True of any loaded feeder (tapering), not the difference from a ring.
(d) ✔ A fault interrupts supply to all consumers beyond the fault…: correct answer.

1.question: A distributor carries a constant current I. If its length is doubled while the conductor cross-section is unchanged, the voltage drop (for a load at the far end) becomes:
1.explanation:
Voltage drop = I R and R = ρ l/A, so the drop is proportional to the length for a constant current and section. The I²R loss also doubles.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Half the original value: Right if the length were halved.
(b) ✘ Four times the original value: Right if both current and length were doubled.
(c) ✘ The same as before: Right if the length were unchanged.
(d) ✔ Twice the original value: correct answer.

2.question: A 2-wire DC distributor of length 0.5 km carries a uniformly distributed load of total 100 A. The resistance of each conductor is 0.1 Ω/km. The voltage drop at the far end (go and return) is:
2.explanation:
Loop resistance for 0.5 km = 2 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.1 Ω. For a uniformly distributed load, drop = I R/2 = 100 × 0.1/2 = 5 V. The full-load-at-the-end drop would be 10 V.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 5 V: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 20 V: Right for a 2 km distributor.
(c) ✘ 2.5 V: Is half: single-conductor resistance only.
(d) ✘ 10 V: Is the drop if the whole 100 A were taken at the far end.

2.question: A 2-wire distributor AB, 400 m long, is fed at both ends at 230 V. A single load of 80 A is tapped at a point 100 m from A. The loop resistance is 0.2 Ω/km. The voltage at the load point is:
2.explanation:
The current from A = 80 × 300/400 = 60 A (the current from B is 20 A). Loop resistance from A to the load = 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02 Ω. Drop = 60 × 0.02 = 1.2 V. V = 230 − 1.2 = 228.8 V. Check from B: 20 A × (0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06 Ω) = 1.2 V.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 229.2 V: Right for 40 A coming from end A (drop 0.8 V).
(b) ✘ 226.0 V: Right if the current from A were 200 A.
(c) ✔ 228.8 V: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 227.6 V: Right if the loop resistance were 0.4 Ω/km.

2.question: The main advantage of a ring-main distribution system over a radial system is that:
options: It has no sectionalising switches, which makes it cheaper
Each load can be fed from both directions, so a faulty section can be isolated
It gives a lower fault level in the distribution network
It needs less copper and cheaper switchgear than a radial system
2.explanation:
In a ring main, any point is fed from two paths, so a fault or maintenance on one section can be isolated with sectionalising switches without loss of supply. The ring needs a more complex protection and the fault level is generally higher, and the cost is greater than that of a radial feeder.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ It has no sectionalising switches, which makes it cheaper: A ring has sectionalising switches; it is not cheaper because of that.
(b) ✔ Each load can be fed from both directions, so a faulty sect…: correct answer.
(c) ✘ It gives a lower fault level in the distribution network: The fault level in a ring is generally higher.
(d) ✘ It needs less copper and cheaper switchgear than a radial s…: A ring needs more copper and switchgear.

2.question: A single-phase 230 V feeder has a total (go and return) resistance of 0.05 Ω and reactance of 0.1 Ω. It supplies a 10 kW load at a power factor of 0.8 lagging at 230 V. The approximate voltage drop in the feeder is:
2.explanation:
I = 10 000/(230 × 0.8) = 54.35 A. ΔV ≈ I(R cos φ + X sin φ) = 54.35 × (0.05 × 0.8 + 0.1 × 0.6) = 54.35 × 0.10 = 5.43 V.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 11.0 V: Is about twice the answer, with R and X counted twice.
(b) ✘ 2.2 V: Is only the R cos φ part; the X sin φ part is left out.
(c) ✘ 10.9 V: Is about twice the answer: right if R and X were doubled.
(d) ✔ 5.4 V: correct answer.

2.question: According to Kelvin's law, the most economical cross-section of a conductor is that for which:
options: The total annual cost of the conductor and its energy loss is exactly zero
The current density equals the maximum allowed by thermal limits
The voltage drop is exactly 5% of the sending-end voltage
The annual cost of energy lost equals the annual charges on the variable part of the capital cost
2.explanation:
Total annual cost = (a + b A) + (c/A). The minimum with respect to the area A is when b A = c/A, i.e. the variable part of the annual capital charges equals the annual cost of the energy lost. The result gives the economical current density, which is then checked against the voltage drop and thermal limits.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The total annual cost of the conductor and its energy loss…: The cost is never zero.
(b) ✘ The current density equals the maximum allowed by thermal l…: Thermal current density is a limit, not Kelvin's condition.
(c) ✘ The voltage drop is exactly 5% of the sending-end voltage: Voltage drop is a separate check, not Kelvin's condition.
(d) ✔ The annual cost of energy lost equals the annual charges on…: correct answer.

2.question: A single-core cable has a conductor of diameter 2 cm, a sheath of inside diameter 5 cm and an insulation of relative permittivity 3.5. The capacitance per km is approximately:
2.explanation:
C = 2π ε0 εr / ln(D/d) = 2π × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 3.5 / ln 2.5 = 1.947 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.9163 = 2.125 × 10⁻¹⁰ F/m = 0.2125 μF/km. Using log10 in place of ln gives 0.489 μF/km.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.489 μF/km: Uses log10 instead of the natural log.
(b) ✔ 0.212 μF/km: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 0.106 μF/km: Uses π instead of 2π.
(d) ✘ 0.061 μF/km: Leaves out εr (0.2125/3.5).

2.question: A single-core cable (conductor radius 1 cm, inner sheath radius 2.5 cm) operates at 33 kV line-to-line in a 3-phase system. The maximum (peak) electric stress in the insulation is approximately:
2.explanation:
Phase voltage (rms) = 33/√3 = 19.05 kV, peak = 26.94 kV. g_max = V/(r ln(R/r)) = 26.94/(1 × ln 2.5) = 29.4 kV/cm (peak). 20.8 is the rms value and 67.7 comes from using log10.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 10.7 kV/cm: Uses D/d = 2.5 directly instead of ln 2.5.
(b) ✘ 20.8 kV/cm: Is the rms value of the stress, not the peak.
(c) ✘ 67.7 kV/cm: Uses log10 instead of the natural log.
(d) ✔ 29.4 kV/cm: correct answer.

2.question: A cable of length 5 km has a core of diameter 1.5 cm and an inner sheath diameter of 3.0 cm. The resistivity of the insulation is 10¹² Ω·m. The insulation resistance is approximately:
2.explanation:
R = (ρ/2πl) ln(D/d) = (10¹²/(2π × 5000)) × ln 2 = 3.183 × 10⁷ × 0.693 = 2.2 × 10⁷ Ω = 22 MΩ. The insulation resistance falls with the length (110 MΩ is the value per km).

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 22.1 MΩ: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 44.1 MΩ: Uses π instead of 2π.
(c) ✘ 9.6 MΩ: Uses log10(2) instead of ln 2.
(d) ✘ 110 MΩ: Is the value per km.

2.question: In capacitance grading of a cable with two layers of insulation of different permittivity, the dielectric placed next to the core should be the one with:
2.explanation:
The electric stress at a radius x is inversely proportional to ε x. Putting the highest-permittivity dielectric near the core reduces the stress where it is the largest, so the stress is distributed more uniformly. The practical difficulty is that high-ε materials are generally less strong.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The lowest dielectric strength: The lowest-strength dielectric would fail first at the core.
(b) ✘ The lowest relative permittivity: Lowest ε next to the core would raise the stress where it is already greatest.
(c) ✔ The highest relative permittivity: correct answer.
(d) ✘ The highest resistivity only: Resistivity does not decide the grading; permittivity does.

2.question: A 3-phase, 11 kV, 50 Hz cable is 20 km long with a capacitance (line-to-neutral) of 0.25 μF/km. The charging current per phase is approximately:
2.explanation:
C = 0.25 × 20 = 5 μF per phase. Ic = 2π f C V_ph = 314.16 × 5 × 10⁻⁶ × (11 000/√3) = 314.16 × 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 6351 = 9.98 A. Using the line voltage in place of the phase voltage gives 17.3 A.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 17.3 A: Uses the line voltage 11 kV instead of the phase voltage.
(b) ✔ 9.98 A: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 0.5 A: Is the current per km.
(d) ✘ 99.8 A: Decimal slip, ten times too large.

1.question: In a load flow study, the slack (swing) bus is the bus at which the following quantities are specified:
options: Voltage magnitude |V| and voltage angle δ
Real power P and voltage magnitude |V|
Real power P and reactive power Q
Reactive power Q and voltage angle δ
1.explanation:
At the slack bus |V| and δ (usually 1.0∠0°) are specified; P and Q are the unknowns, which are found at the end of the solution. The slack bus supplies the difference between the total load plus losses and the scheduled generation. Specifying P and Q is the PQ (load) bus; specifying P and |V| is the PV (generator) bus.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ Voltage magnitude |V| and voltage angle δ: correct answer.
(b) ✘ Real power P and voltage magnitude |V|: P and |V| are specified at a PV bus.
(c) ✘ Real power P and reactive power Q: P and Q are specified at a PQ bus.
(d) ✘ Reactive power Q and voltage angle δ: Q and δ are not specified together at any bus type.

1.question: At a generator (PV) bus in a load flow problem, the specified and unknown quantities are:
options: Specified: P and Q; unknown: |V| and δ
Specified: |V| and δ; unknown: P and Q
Specified: P and |V|; unknown: Q and δ
Specified: Q and δ; unknown: P and |V|
1.explanation:
A voltage-controlled generator bus has its real power output (turbine setting) and terminal voltage magnitude (excitation) fixed. The reactive power Q it must deliver and the angle δ come out of the solution.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Specified: P and Q; unknown: |V| and δ: P and Q specified: that is a PQ bus.
(b) ✘ Specified: |V| and δ; unknown: P and Q: |V| and δ specified: that is the slack bus.
(c) ✔ Specified: P and |V|; unknown: Q and δ: correct answer.
(d) ✘ Specified: Q and δ; unknown: P and |V|: Q and δ are not specified together at any bus type.

1.question: A power system has n buses, with one slack bus and the remaining buses all PQ buses. The number of real (simultaneous) power-flow equations to be solved in polar form is:
1.explanation:
Every PQ bus gives two unknowns (|V|, δ) and two real equations (P and Q balance). With n − 1 such buses the number of equations is 2(n − 1). For a 5-bus system this is 8.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ n: Is the number of buses, not equations.
(b) ✘ 2n: Counts the slack bus as well.
(c) ✘ n − 1: Right if only P equations were needed (all non-slack buses PV).
(d) ✔ 2(n − 1): correct answer.

1.question: In the Newton–Raphson load flow (polar form) of a 5-bus system with 1 slack bus, 2 PV buses and 2 PQ buses, the size of the Jacobian matrix is:
1.explanation:
Unknown angles: δ at all non-slack buses = 4. Unknown magnitudes: |V| at the PQ buses only = 2. Total unknowns = 6, so the Jacobian is 6 × 6 (P equations at 4 buses, Q equations at 2 PQ buses). Using 8 × 8 would wrongly treat the PV buses as PQ buses.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 4 × 4: Right for the P–δ part alone (4 angles).
(b) ✔ 6 × 6: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 8 × 8: Treats all four non-slack buses as PQ (2 × 4).
(d) ✘ 10 × 10: Treats all five buses as PQ (2 × 5).

1.question: In the fast decoupled load flow (FDLF) method applied to a 6-bus system with 1 slack bus, 2 PV buses and 3 PQ buses, the sizes of the B′ and B″ matrices are respectively:
1.explanation:
B′ relates ΔP/|V| to Δδ and has one row for every non-slack bus: 6 − 1 = 5. B″ relates ΔQ/|V| to Δ|V| and has one row for every PQ bus only: 3. Both are real and are constant, so they are inverted (factorised) once.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 5 × 5 and 5 × 5: B″ is 5 × 5 only if all non-slack buses were PQ.
(b) ✘ 6 × 6 and 6 × 6: Includes the slack bus, which is not solved.
(c) ✔ 5 × 5 and 3 × 3: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 3 × 3 and 5 × 5: Swaps B′ and B″.

1.question: Which one of the following statements about the Gauss–Seidel (GS) and Newton–Raphson (NR) load flow methods is correct?
options: NR needs far fewer iterations than GS, almost independent of system size
GS converges quadratically, whereas NR converges only linearly
NR cannot be applied when a system has generator (PV) buses
GS needs the Jacobian matrix to be recomputed in each iteration
1.explanation:
NR has quadratic convergence near the solution and takes about 3–5 iterations for large systems regardless of size; each iteration costs more because of the Jacobian. GS has linear convergence and the number of iterations increases roughly with the number of buses, but each iteration is cheap and no Jacobian is required. Both handle PV buses.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ NR needs far fewer iterations than GS, almost independent o…: correct answer.
(b) ✘ GS converges quadratically, whereas NR converges only linea…: Reversed: NR converges quadratically and GS linearly.
(c) ✘ NR cannot be applied when a system has generator (PV) buses: NR handles PV buses easily (the Q rows are dropped).
(d) ✘ GS needs the Jacobian matrix to be recomputed in each itera…: NR recomputes the Jacobian; GS has no Jacobian.

1.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the fast decoupled load flow method?
options: The bus voltage magnitudes are close to 1.0 pu
The angle differences between adjacent buses are small
The line resistances are much larger than the line reactances
P is mainly coupled with δ and Q with |V|
1.explanation:
FDLF is based on (i) R ≪ X (typical of high-voltage lines), (ii) small angle differences so that cos δ ≈ 1 and sin δ ≈ δ, and (iii) |V| ≈ 1 pu. Together these make the P–δ and Q–|V| problems decoupled. So 'R much larger than X' is the opposite of the assumption.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The bus voltage magnitudes are close to 1.0 pu: This is an assumption of FDLF (|V| ≈ 1 pu).
(b) ✘ The angle differences between adjacent buses are small: This is an assumption of FDLF (small angle differences).
(c) ✔ The line resistances are much larger than the line reactanc…: correct answer.
(d) ✘ P is mainly coupled with δ and Q with |V|: This is an assumption of FDLF (P–δ and Q–V decoupling).

1.question: In a DC load flow, the real power flowing from bus 1 to bus 2 through a lossless line of reactance X12 = 0.2 pu is P12 = (δ1 − δ2)/X12. If δ1 = 0 and δ2 = −0.1 rad, P12 is:
1.explanation:
P12 = (0 − (−0.1))/0.2 = 0.1/0.2 = 0.5 pu, flowing from bus 1 to bus 2 (positive, since bus 1 leads). A negative sign would mean flow in the opposite direction. The DC load flow assumes |V| = 1 pu, flat voltage, small angles, and R neglected.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ −0.5 pu: Right if δ2 were +0.1 rad (flow reversed).
(b) ✔ 0.5 pu: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 2.0 pu: Right for X = 0.05 pu.
(d) ✘ 0.02 pu: Multiplies by X instead of dividing (0.1 × 0.2).

1.question: The slack bus supplies the total losses of the system in a load flow solution because:
options: The slack bus has the lowest voltage magnitude among all the buses
Losses are unknown until the solution is obtained, so one bus must keep its real power free
The slack bus is always the bus closest to the main load centre of the network
The slack bus is always the generator with the largest capacity in the system
1.explanation:
Total real power loss = ΣPG − ΣPD is not known until the voltages and angles are solved. If every generator had its P specified, the power balance could not be met in general. So one bus (the slack) has its P left unspecified to take up the mismatch, i.e. it generates the losses. The slack bus is not chosen by location or voltage level.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ The slack bus has the lowest voltage magnitude among all th…: The slack voltage is specified (1.0 pu), not the lowest.
(b) ✔ Losses are unknown until the solution is obtained, so one b…: correct answer.
(c) ✘ The slack bus is always the bus closest to the main load ce…: Location does not decide it.
(d) ✘ The slack bus is always the generator with the largest capa…: The largest unit is a common choice, but that is not why it supplies the losses.

1.question: During a load flow solution a PV bus is found to need reactive power beyond the maximum Q limit of its generator. The usual treatment is to:
options: Keep |V| fixed and ignore the limit
Remove the generator from the network
Treat it as the slack bus and fix the angle
Treat it as a PQ bus with Q held at Qmax; |V| then floats
1.explanation:
A generator cannot supply more than Qmax. Once the limit is violated, Q is held at Qmax (the bus becomes PQ) and |V| is no longer held; it will normally fall below the scheduled value. If the Q later returns inside the limit with the voltage above its set value, the bus can be switched back to PV.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ Keep |V| fixed and ignore the limit: Right only if the limit has not been reached.
(b) ✘ Remove the generator from the network: Removing the machine is not done.
(c) ✘ Treat it as the slack bus and fix the angle: Only one slack bus exists; a limit-hit bus becomes PQ.
(d) ✔ Treat it as a PQ bus with Q held at Qmax; |V| then floats: correct answer.

2.question: Refer to the figure. All line resistances are zero and the line reactances are X12 = 0.1, X13 = 0.2 and X23 = 0.2 pu. The elements Y22 and Y23 of the bus admittance matrix are respectively:
2.explanation:
Line admittances: y12 = 1/(j0.1) = −j10, y13 = 1/(j0.2) = −j5, y23 = −j5. Y22 = y12 + y23 = −j10 − j5 = −j15. Y23 = −y23 = +j5 (off-diagonal elements are the negative of the line admittance). The diagonal element for an inductive network is negative imaginary and the off-diagonal elements are positive imaginary.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ −j10 pu and +j5 pu: Y22 would be −j10 if only line 1–2 were attached.
(b) ✘ −j15 pu and −j5 pu: Off-diagonal sign wrong: Y23 = −y23 = +j5.
(c) ✔ −j15 pu and +j5 pu: correct answer.
(d) ✘ +j15 pu and −j5 pu: Both signs reversed.

2.question: Bus 1 is the slack bus with V1 = 1.0∠0° pu. Bus 2 is a load bus (S2 = 0.5 + j0.2 pu drawn from the network) joined to bus 1 by a line of impedance z = 0.1 + j0.3 pu. Starting from a flat start V2⁽⁰⁾ = 1.0 + j0, the value of V2 after the first Gauss–Seidel iteration is:
2.explanation:
For a PQ bus, V2 = (1/Y22)[(P2 − jQ2)/V2* − Y21 V1] with Y22 = y, Y21 = −y, y = 1/z. Since the bus is a load, P2 = −0.5 and Q2 = −0.2, so P2 − jQ2 = −0.5 + j0.2. Then V2 = z(−0.5 + j0.2)/1.0 + 1.0. z(−0.5 + j0.2) = (0.1 + j0.3)(−0.5 + j0.2) = −0.05 + j0.02 − j0.15 − 0.06 = −0.11 − j0.13. So V2 = 0.89 − j0.13 (|V2| = 0.899 pu). Using +0.5 and +0.2 (generation sign) gives the wrong answer 1.11 + j0.13.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.89 + j0.13 pu: Sign of the imaginary part wrong.
(b) ✘ 0.95 − j0.05 pu: Not from the Gauss–Seidel update.
(c) ✘ 1.11 + j0.13 pu: Treats the load as generation (sign of S reversed).
(d) ✔ 0.89 − j0.13 pu: correct answer.

2.question: A load of P2 = 1.0 pu is connected to bus 2, which is joined to the slack bus (V1 = 1∠0°) by a lossless line of X = 0.2 pu. In the Newton–Raphson method with flat start (V2 = 1.0, δ2 = 0), only the P2–δ2 equation is solved and ∂P2/∂δ2 is evaluated at the flat start. The correction Δδ2 after the first iteration is:
2.explanation:
At the flat start the calculated power P2 = (V1V2/X) sin(δ2 − δ1) = 0, so ΔP2 = P2,spec − P2,calc = −1.0 − 0 = −1.0 (a load is negative injection). The Jacobian element is ∂P2/∂δ2 = (V1V2/X) cos δ2 = 1/0.2 = 5. Δδ2 = ΔP2/J = −1.0/5 = −0.2 rad = −11.46°. The negative sign shows that the load bus lags the slack bus, as expected for a bus that draws power.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ +11.46°: Sign wrong: a load makes δ2 negative.
(b) ✔ −11.46°: correct answer.
(c) ✘ −5.73°: Half the angle: right if ∂P/∂δ were twice as large.
(d) ✘ −0.2°: Is the right value in radians (−0.2 rad), not in degrees.

2.question: Refer to the figure. Bus 1 is the slack (V1 = 1∠0°), and loads of P2 = 1.0 pu and P3 = 0.2 pu are connected at buses 2 and 3. Using the DC load flow, the voltage angle δ2 is:
2.explanation:
With the slack bus as reference, [B′][δ] = [P] where B′22 = 1/0.1 + 1/0.2 = 15, B′33 = 1/0.2 + 1/0.2 = 10 and B′23 = −5. So [15 −5; −5 10][δ2; δ3] = [−1.0; −0.2]. Determinant = 150 − 25 = 125. δ2 = (10(−1.0) + 5(−0.2))/125 = −11/125 = −0.088 rad, δ3 = (5(−1.0) + 15(−0.2))/125 = −8/125 = −0.064 rad. (−0.064 is δ3.)

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ −0.064 rad: Is δ3, not δ2.
(b) ✘ −0.120 rad: Not from solving [B′][δ] = [P].
(c) ✔ −0.088 rad: correct answer.
(d) ✘ −0.200 rad: Right for a single 0.2 pu line carrying 1 pu.

2.question: Refer to the figure (bus 1 slack, V1 = 1∠0°, X12 = 0.1, X13 = 0.2, X23 = 0.2 pu). Loads P2 = 1.0 pu and P3 = 0.2 pu are connected at buses 2 and 3, and the DC load flow gives δ2 = −0.088 rad and δ3 = −0.064 rad. The real power flowing in line 1–2 from bus 1 towards bus 2 is:
2.explanation:
P12 = (δ1 − δ2)/X12 = (0 + 0.088)/0.1 = 0.88 pu. In the same way P13 = (0 + 0.064)/0.2 = 0.32 pu. The sum P12 + P13 = 1.20 pu = P2 + P3, which is the total load supplied by the slack bus (a lossless model). 0.32 is the flow in line 1–3.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 0.88 pu: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 1.00 pu: Is the load at bus 2, not the flow in line 1–2.
(c) ✘ 0.64 pu: Mixes δ3 (0.064) with X12.
(d) ✘ 0.32 pu: Is the flow in line 1–3.

2.question: Refer to the figure (X23 = 0.2 pu). In a DC load flow of this network the bus angles are found to be δ2 = −0.088 rad and δ3 = −0.064 rad (loads P2 = 1.0 pu, P3 = 0.2 pu). The real power in line 2–3 is:
options: 0.024 pu flowing from bus 2 to bus 3
0.12 pu flowing from bus 2 to bus 3
0.12 pu flowing from bus 3 to bus 2
0.20 pu flowing from bus 3 to bus 2
2.explanation:
P23 = (δ2 − δ3)/X23 = (−0.088 + 0.064)/0.2 = −0.12 pu. The negative sign means the flow is from bus 3 to bus 2. Check at bus 2: P12 + P32 = 0.88 + 0.12 = 1.0 = load at bus 2. At bus 3: P13 − P32 = 0.32 − 0.12 = 0.2 = load at bus 3. So the heavier load at bus 2 draws power through both paths.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.024 pu flowing from bus 2 to bus 3: Forgets to divide by X, and the direction is wrong.
(b) ✘ 0.12 pu flowing from bus 2 to bus 3: Right magnitude, wrong direction.
(c) ✔ 0.12 pu flowing from bus 3 to bus 2: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 0.20 pu flowing from bus 3 to bus 2: Is the load at bus 3, not the line flow.

2.question: In a Gauss–Seidel load flow a bus voltage has a previous value 1.0 pu and the new value calculated is 0.90 pu (both real, for simplicity). Using an acceleration factor α = 1.6, the accelerated value used for the next step is:
2.explanation:
V(accelerated) = V(old) + α[V(new) − V(old)] = 1.0 + 1.6(0.90 − 1.0) = 1.0 − 0.16 = 0.84 pu. α = 1 gives the normal GS value (0.90). A factor 1.4 to 1.7 usually speeds up convergence for load flow problems; too large a factor causes divergence.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.94 pu: Right for α = 0.6 (deceleration).
(b) ✔ 0.84 pu: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 0.96 pu: Right for α = 0.4.
(d) ✘ 0.90 pu: Right for α = 1 (no acceleration).

2.question: At a PV bus in the Gauss–Seidel method, the computed voltage in an iteration is 0.98 + j0.12 pu while the scheduled magnitude is 1.02 pu. The corrected voltage used in the next step is approximately:
2.explanation:
Only the angle of the computed voltage is retained and the magnitude is reset to the scheduled value. Angle = tan⁻¹(0.12/0.98) = 6.98°. Corrected V = 1.02(cos 6.98° + j sin 6.98°) = 1.02(0.9926 + j0.1215) = 1.012 + j0.124 pu. Simply replacing the real part (1.02 + j0.12) would give a magnitude of 1.027, not 1.02.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 1.02 + j0.00 pu: Right if the angle were also reset to zero.
(b) ✔ 1.012 + j0.124 pu: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 0.98 + j0.12 pu: Is the uncorrected computed value.
(d) ✘ 1.02 + j0.12 pu: Resets the real part only, not the magnitude.

2.question: Two buses are connected by a lossless line of X = 0.1 pu. V1 = 1.0∠0° and V2 = 0.95∠−5° pu. The real power P12 and reactive power Q12 flowing from bus 1 into the line are approximately:
2.explanation:
P12 = (V1V2/X) sin(δ1 − δ2) = (1 × 0.95/0.1) sin 5° = 9.5 × 0.08716 = 0.828 pu. Q12 = (V1/X)(V1 − V2 cos(δ1 − δ2)) = (1/0.1)(1 − 0.95 × 0.99619) = 10 × 0.05362 = 0.536 pu. Both are positive: bus 1 sends real and reactive power to bus 2 (bus 1 is at the higher voltage magnitude and leads in angle).

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ P12 = 0.083 pu and Q12 = 0.536 pu: P value is ten times too small.
(b) ✘ P12 = 0.828 pu and Q12 = 0.104 pu: Q uses the wrong formula.
(c) ✘ P12 = 0.536 pu and Q12 = 0.828 pu: P and Q are swapped.
(d) ✔ P12 = 0.828 pu and Q12 = 0.536 pu: correct answer.

2.question: Two buses are joined by a line of X = 0.1 pu and no resistance, with V1 = 1.0∠0° and V2 = 0.95∠−5° pu. The reactive power loss in the line is approximately:
2.explanation:
Q12 = 0.536 pu leaves bus 1. At bus 2, Q21 = (V2/X)(V2 − V1 cos δ) = (0.95/0.1)(0.95 − 0.99619) = −0.439 pu, i.e. 0.439 pu is delivered from the line into bus 2. Loss = Q12 + Q21 = 0.536 − 0.439 = 0.097 pu. Check with I²X = |V1 − V2|²/X = 0.00973/0.1 = 0.097 pu. The real power loss is zero because the line has no resistance (P12 + P21 = 0.828 − 0.828 = 0).

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 0.097 pu: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 0.439 pu: Is the Q received at bus 2.
(c) ✘ 0.000 pu: Right for a line with no reactance (X = 0).
(d) ✘ 0.536 pu: Is the Q leaving bus 1, not the loss.

1.question: A 3-phase transformer is rated 20 MVA, 33/11 kV, with a reactance of 8% on its own rating. Expressed in per unit on a new base of 50 MVA (same voltage), its reactance is:
1.explanation:
Per-unit reactance scales directly with the MVA base ratio when voltage is unchanged: X_new = X_old x (MVA_new/MVA_old) = 0.08 x (50/20) = 0.20 pu.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.08 pu: Right if the base were unchanged.
(b) ✘ 0.16 pu: Right for a new base of 40 MVA.
(c) ✔ 0.20 pu: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 0.32 pu: Right for a new base of 80 MVA.

1.question: At a bus with a base of 100 MVA and 11 kV (line-to-line), the base current is approximately:
1.explanation:
Base current = MVA_base / (sqrt(3) x kV_base) = 100 / (1.732 x 11) is approximately 5.25 kA.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 2.62 kA: Right for a 50 MVA base.
(b) ✔ 5.25 kA: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 9.09 kA: Is 100/11, forgetting √3.
(d) ✘ 10.5 kA: Right for a 200 MVA base.

1.question: For a system with a base of 100 MVA and 132 kV (line), the base impedance is approximately:
1.explanation:
Base impedance = (kV_base)^2 / MVA_base = 132^2 / 100 = 17424/100 is approximately 174.2 ohm.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 17.4 ohm: Decimal slip, ten times too small.
(b) ✘ 87.1 ohm: Right for a 200 MVA base.
(c) ✔ 174.2 ohm: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 348.5 ohm: Right for a 50 MVA base.

2.question: Refer to the attached single line diagram. A generator is rated 100 MVA, 11 kV with reactance 0.18 pu on its own base. Choosing a new system base of 200 MVA (same voltage on the generator side), the generator's reactance on the new base is:
2.explanation:
X_new = X_old x (MVA_new/MVA_old) x (kV_old/kV_new)^2. Since the generator's own voltage (11 kV) matches the system's LV-side base voltage, the voltage ratio term = 1. X_new = 0.18 x (200/100) x 1 = 0.36 pu.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.18 pu: Right if the base were unchanged.
(b) ✘ 0.24 pu: Right for a 133 MVA base.
(c) ✔ 0.36 pu: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 0.45 pu: Right for a 250 MVA base.

2.question: Refer to the attached single line diagram. The transformer is rated 100 MVA, 11/220 kV with reactance 0.10 pu on its own base. On a new system base of 200 MVA, with the generator's reactance already converted to 0.36 pu (previous question), the fault MVA for a three-phase fault at point F (pre-fault voltage 1.0 pu) is approximately:
2.explanation:
Transformer's reactance on the new base: X_new = 0.10 x (200/100) x (220/220)^2 = 0.20 pu. Total reactance (generator + transformer in series) = 0.36 + 0.20 = 0.56 pu. Fault MVA = Base MVA / X_total = 200 / 0.56 is approximately 357.1 MVA.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 178.6 MVA: Uses a 100 MVA base with the 200 MVA reactances.
(b) ✘ 267.9 MVA: Uses a 150 MVA base.
(c) ✔ 357.1 MVA: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 400.0 MVA: Right if X_total were 0.50 pu.

1.question: A 3-phase, 25 MVA, 11 kV alternator has a subtransient reactance of 0.20 pu on its own base. It is connected through a step-up transformer (25 MVA, 11/110 kV, reactance 0.08 pu) and a transmission line (reactance 0.12 pu, same base) to a fault point F on the 110 kV side. Pre-fault voltage is 1.0 pu. The fault current for a three-phase symmetrical fault at F is approximately:
1.explanation:
Solution : 
Total reactance = 0.20 + 0.08 + 0.12 = 0.40 pu 
(all on 25 MVA, 110 kV base).
Base current on 110 kV side = 25 / (√3 × 110) = 0.1312 kA.
Fault current = (1.0 / 0.40) × 0.1312 = 2.5 × 0.1312 ≈ 0.328 kA.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.16 kA: Right for X = 0.8 pu.
(b) ✔ 0.33 kA: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 0.66 kA: Right for X = 0.20 pu (generator alone).
(d) ✘ 1.31 kA: Is the base current on the 11 kV side, the wrong side.

1.question: At a certain bus in a power system, the positive, negative, and zero sequence reactances are X1 = 0.20 pu, X2 = 0.20 pu, and X0 = 0.10 pu (on a 100 MVA, 11 kV base). Pre-fault voltage is 1.0 pu. The fault current for a single line-to-ground (L-G) fault at this bus (zero fault impedance) is approximately:
1.explanation:
For a bolted L-G fault: Ia1 = Ia2 = Ia0 = V / (X1+X2+X0) = 1 / 0.50 = 2.0 pu.
Fault current = 3 × Ia1 = 6.0 pu.
Base current = 100 / (√3 × 11) = 5.249 kA.
Fault current = 6.0 × 5.249 ≈ 31.5 kA

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 10.5 kA: Is Ia1 alone; the factor 3 is missing.
(b) ✘ 15.7 kA: Right if X0 were 0.6 pu.
(c) ✘ 21.0 kA: Right if X0 were 0.35 pu.
(d) ✔ 31.5 kA: correct answer.

1.question: For a three-phase symmetrical (bolted) fault at a bus, which sequence network(s) carry fault current?
1.explanation:
A three-phase fault is balanced across all three phases, so by definition only the positive-sequence network carries current — negative and zero sequence currents are zero for a perfectly symmetrical fault.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ Positive sequence network only: correct answer.
(b) ✘ Positive and negative sequence networks: Right for a line-to-line fault.
(c) ✘ All three sequence networks equally: Right for a line-to-ground fault (all three in series).
(d) ✘ Zero sequence network only: Never: zero-sequence current alone needs an unbalanced earth fault.

1.question: At a fault point, X1 = X2 = 0.25 pu, pre-fault voltage is 1.0 pu, and the base current is 5.0 kA. The fault current magnitude for a line-to-line (L-L) fault is approximately:
1.explanation:
For a bolted L-L fault: Ia1 = -Ia2 = V / (X1+X2) = 1 / 0.50 = 2.0 pu.
Fault current magnitude = √3 × Ia1 = √3 × 2.0 ≈ 3.464 pu.
Fault current = 3.464 × 5.0 ≈ 17.3 kA.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 8.7 kA: Right if X1 + X2 were 1.0 pu.
(b) ✘ 10.0 kA: Is the sequence current Ia1 without the √3 factor.
(c) ✔ 17.3 kA: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 20.0 kA: Is the three-phase fault current (1/0.25 × 5 kA).

1.question: At a fault location, X1 = X2 = 0.30 pu. If the zero-sequence reactance X0 is significantly SMALLER than X1, which statement is generally true?
options: The single line-to-ground fault current can exceed the three-phase fault current
The line-to-line fault current always exceeds the three-phase fault current
The double line-to-ground fault current is always the smallest of all fault types
Fault current magnitude is independent of X0
1.explanation:
3-phase fault current = V/X1 (constant regardless of X0).
LG fault current = 3V / (2X1 + X0) — this grows larger as X0 shrinks.
Worked check: with X1=0.30, if X0=0.10, LG current = 4.29 pu > 3-phase current = 3.33 pu.
So when X0 is small relative to X1 (a solidly grounded, low-impedance-path system), the LG fault can genuinely exceed the three-phase fault current - this is why some grounded systems must be rated for LG fault current as the worst case, not just the 3-phase fault.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ The single line-to-ground fault current can exceed the thre…: correct answer.
(b) ✘ The line-to-line fault current always exceeds the three-pha…: The line-to-line fault current is below the three-phase value (√3/2 of it).
(c) ✘ The double line-to-ground fault current is always the small…: The L-L fault is the smallest; L-L-G is not.
(d) ✘ Fault current magnitude is independent of X0: Ground-fault currents depend strongly on X0.

1.question: At a fault point, X1 = X2 = 0.25 pu and X0 = 0.20 pu, with pre-fault voltage 1.0 pu. For a double line-to-ground (L-L-G) fault, the positive-sequence fault current component (Ia1) is approximately:
1.explanation:
Ia1 = V / [X1 + (X2 × X0)/(X2 + X0)]
Parallel combination of X2 and X0 = (0.25 × 0.20)/(0.25+0.20) = 0.1111 pu.
Ia1 = 1 / (0.25 + 0.1111) = 1 / 0.3611 ≈ 2.77 pu.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 1.85 pu: Not from the parallel combination of X2 and X0.
(b) ✘ 2.22 pu: Is 1/(X1 + X0): ignores X2 in parallel.
(c) ✔ 2.77 pu: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 3.33 pu: Is not the result of the correct sequence-network combination.

1.question: A 3-phase transformer is rated 20 MVA, 33/11 kV, with a reactance of 8% on its own rating. Expressed in per unit on a new base of 50 MVA (same voltage), its reactance is:
1.explanation:
Solution 1: Per-unit reactance scales directly with the MVA base ratio when voltage is unchanged: X_new = X_old x (MVA_new/MVA_old) = 0.08 x (50/20) = 0.20 pu.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 0.08 pu: Right if the base were unchanged.
(b) ✘ 0.16 pu: Right for a new base of 40 MVA.
(c) ✔ 0.20 pu: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 0.32 pu: Right for a new base of 80 MVA.

1.question: At a bus with a base of 100 MVA and 11 kV (line-to-line), the base current is approximately:
1.explanation:
Solution 2: Base current = MVA_base / (sqrt(3) x kV_base) = 100 / (1.732 x 11) is approximately 5.25 kA.

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 2.62 kA: Right for a 50 MVA base.
(b) ✔ 5.25 kA: correct answer.
(c) ✘ 9.09 kA: Is 100/11, forgetting √3.
(d) ✘ 10.5 kA: Right for a 200 MVA base.

1.question: For a system with a base of 100 MVA and 132 kV (line), the base impedance is approximately:
1.explanation:
Solution 3: 
Base impedance = (kV_base)^2 / MVA_base = 132^2 / 100 = 17424/100 is approximately 174.2 ohm

Why the other options?
(a) ✘ 17.4 ohm: Decimal slip, ten times too small.
(b) ✘ 87.1 ohm: Right for a 200 MVA base.
(c) ✔ 174.2 ohm: correct answer.
(d) ✘ 348.5 ohm: Right for a 50 MVA base.

1.question: Refer to the attached phasor diagram. In symmetrical component theory, the operator 'a' represents a phase shift of:
1.explanation:
The operator a is defined as a = 1 angle 120 degrees - a unit-magnitude phasor that rotates any quantity it multiplies by exactly 120 degrees. a-squared = 1 angle 240 degrees, and a-cubed = 1 angle 360 degrees = 1.

Why the other options?
(a) ✔ 120 degrees: correct answer.
(b) ✘ 90 degrees: Is the operator j.
(c) ✘ 240 degrees: Is a².
(d) ✘ 180 degrees: Is −1.

1.question: For a perfectly balanced three-phase system (equal magnitudes, 120 degrees apart), the negative-sequence and zero-sequence components are:
options: Both equal to the positive-sequence component
